item.title: Sentinel‐2 in PRODES : Enhancing Cerrado Vegetation Suppression Mapping
item.description:
Andrea D. Scheide, Taise F. Pinheiro, Magog A. de Carvalho, Vagner Luis Camilotti, Izaias de Souza Silva, Luciana de S. Soler, João Felipe S. K. C. Pinto, Marcos Adami, et al.
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70436
ABSTRACT The PRODES Cerrado system provides annual mapping of native vegetation suppression for Brazil's tropical savanna but has historically relied on 30 m Landsat imagery without systematically assessing higher‐resolution alternatives. This reliance may limit the detection of small or early‐stage clearings, particularly in heterogeneous and cloud‐prone regions. To address this, we compared Landsat‐8/OLI and Sentinel‐2/MSI imagery under three configurations—single‐date Landsat‐8, single‐date Sentinel‐2, and 16‐day Sentinel‐2 mosaics (Brazil Data Cube)—within the PRODES framework. Results indicate that vegetation structure interacts with spatial resolution, deforestation dynamics, and temporal variability to influence detectability. Among all tested configurations, the 16‐day Sentinel‐2 mosaics achieved the best balance between spatial detail and temporal coverage, supporting its operational adoption by PRODES Cerrado for consistent, large‐scale vegetation suppression mapping.

item.title: Expert Knowledge–Driven Hybrid Fuzzy Logic Modeling of Heat‐Related Illnesses
item.description:
Ehsan Foroutan, Tao Hu
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70444
ABSTRACT Extreme heat poses significant public health risks, particularly in rapidly urbanizing cities, and creates broad challenges for society. Traditional statistical and machine learning models are widely used to estimate heat‐related health outcomes, but their limited interpretability, high data requirements, and difficulty in incorporating expert knowledge, especially in data‐scarce settings, create key challenges for heat‐health modeling. To advance more sustainable and decision‐ready analytics, this study develops a hybrid fuzzy logic model and compares it with data‐driven and expert knowledge‐driven fuzzy logic–based approaches for estimating heat‐related emergency department visits (EDVs) in two major Texas metropolitan areas: Austin and Dallas–Fort Worth (DFW). The data‐driven model learns fuzzy rules, tunes membership functions, and optimizes rule weights from input–output data; the expert knowledge‐driven model uses domain knowledge to define rule structures; and the hybrid model combines expert rules with data‐driven tuning and optimization. All fuzzy models were evaluated with five‐fold cross‐validation and benchmarked against the best‐performing machine learning model identified in the AutoML framework—FLAML. Results show that in Austin, the hybrid fuzzy model achieved the lowest MAE of 118.73, outperforming the FLAML benchmark (MAE = 125.16), while the best‐performing data‐driven fuzzy model reached an MAE of 89.49. In contrast, in DFW, FLAML delivered the highest accuracy (MAE = 137.90), surpassing all fuzzy configurations. By systematically comparing expert‐driven, data‐driven, and hybrid fuzzy models against a modern AutoML benchmark, this study offers an original contribution that clarifies when and how interpretable, expert‐informed fuzzy systems can complement or exceed black‐box machine learning approaches, and enable agencies to make transparent, equitable, and uncertainty‐aware decisions that strengthen climate resilience and protect society.
